title: Dry-run: a hash ring with virtual nodes

spec.title: Dry-run: a hash ring with virtual nodes
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. Build the naive version first so the interviewer sees the failure, then fix it — that ordering is most of the score.

steps.title: Show the problem before the solution
steps.explain: Write modulo routing first and demonstrate what a single failure does. Leading with the broken version proves you understand why the ring exists rather than that you memorised it.
steps.saysOutLoud: Let me start with the obvious approach and show why it collapses.

steps.title: Place servers on a ring instead
steps.explain: The key move: hash servers into the same space as keys. A server's position depends only on its own name, so it does not shift when other servers come and go — that independence is the entire trick.

steps.title: Look up by walking clockwise
steps.explain: Binary search for the first position at or after the key's hash, wrapping at the end. O(log N) and entirely local — no network hop, which is why every client can hold the ring in memory instead of asking a central service.
steps.saysOutLoud: Lookup is a binary search over a sorted array — no coordination on the read path.

steps.title: Explain why 150 virtual nodes, not 1
steps.explain: Two reasons, and the second matters more in production. Even distribution is the obvious one. The real payoff is that a failed server's load is spread across every survivor instead of dumping entirely onto its single clockwise neighbour — which is what turns one node failure into a cascade.

steps.title: Replication falls out of the same walk
steps.explain: Keep walking for R distinct physical servers. 'Distinct' is load-bearing — a naive walk hands you the same machine repeatedly because it owns many positions, leaving you one copy where you wanted three. Production also skips racks and availability zones.

steps.title: Gossip keeps every client's ring in sync
steps.explain: Membership spreads by gossip rather than a central registry, which means the ring is eventually consistent: during a change, two clients can briefly disagree about who owns a key. The storage layer absorbs that with replicas and read repair instead of trying to make membership instantaneous.

steps.title: Name what the ring does not fix
steps.explain: Get ahead of the standard follow-up. The ring balances key count, not traffic — one celebrity key still lands on one server and still melts it. Saying this unprompted shows you know the boundary of the technique.
steps.saysOutLoud: Consistent hashing balances keys, not load — a hot key is a separate problem.

spec.closing: If they ask for something simpler: rendezvous hashing gives the same minimal-movement guarantee with no ring to maintain, at O(N) per lookup instead of O(log N). Fine for tens of servers, not for thousands.
